site.intro:
I teach and build on Palantir Foundry at Ontologize. Before that I spent three years at Swiss Re in Bengaluru building machine-learning and language-model pipelines for underwriters, and before that I taught Python online and studied operational research at the University of Delhi.

This page is the plain version: what I have worked on, what I have built, and a short explanation of the idea behind each. The [terminal](/) is the playful version.

work.label: Ontologize · Palantir instructor & engineer
work.title: Teaching and building on Palantir Foundry
work.body: Ontologize runs Palantir training, fellowships and exams. I teach Foundry and build with it: how data is modelled into an ontology, how pipelines feed it, and how applications sit on top.

work.label: Swiss Re · Retrieval
work.title: Nebula: answers from a pile of documents
work.body:
Underwriters judge a company by reading its news, filings and financial reports. Nebula lets them ask a question instead. It searches a corpus of company documents for the passages that matter, then has a language model answer from those passages only, so every answer points back to its sources.

I built the PDF ingestion and the semantic search (Python for text extraction, TypeScript for vector search), plus an admin panel for prompts, evaluation and one-click reruns. Research that took days now takes minutes.

figure.caption: Retrieve, then answer. The model only sees the passages the search found.

notes.text: Retrieval-augmented generation: look things up first, then write the answer from what was found.
Search by meaning rather than exact words, by comparing text as vectors.

work.label: Swiss Re · Explainability
work.title: Loss-ratio hotspots
work.body:
A portfolio loses money in some places and not others. We trained a model to predict losses across a portfolio of US agents and lawyers, then used SHAP to ask it which factors drove its predictions: claim frequency, policy tenure, regional risk.

The model was the means; the explanation was the product. It told the business where to look, and the changes that followed brought the loss ratio down by 5%.

figure.caption: Each dot is one policy. Its position shows how far one factor pushed that policy's predicted loss.

notes.text: Claims paid divided by premiums earned. Under 100%, the insurer keeps money.
Splits one prediction into each input's contribution, using an idea from game theory.

plates.title: The terminal on this site
plates.body: The front page of rvs23.dev is a command line over a digital-rain animation drawn on a canvas. The rain is a grid of characters that never moves: each falling stream is a bright cursor that lights cells as it passes, and every cell fades back to black on its own. Plain JavaScript, no framework.

figure.caption: Streams don't move letters. They move brightness down a fixed grid of glyphs.

plates.title: Customer prioritization
plates.body: Which trial users are about to buy? A linear classifier trained with stochastic gradient descent on 50+ behavioural signals scored every user daily, and sales called the top 250 instead of everyone: 83% fewer calls, 63% more conversions. It learned from each day's outcomes without retraining from scratch. Written for Packt Publishing, 2021.

figure.caption: One straight line separates likely buyers from the rest; distance from it becomes the score.

plates.title: rv-markdown-paper
plates.body: A tool that turns a Markdown file into a print-quality PDF with a fixed editorial design: grey paper, one ink, three typefaces. Authors write content and the template does the rest. This page borrows its look.

figure.caption: Markdown in, a typeset PDF out, identical on every machine.

learn.question: How does a web page work?
learn.answer: HTML describes the page and CSS dresses it. The first primer teaches both through this site's own code.

learn.question: How does the falling-code rain work?
learn.answer: A fixed grid, moving brightness, and a loop that runs sixty times a second. The second primer walks through it.

learn.question: What is retrieval-augmented generation?
learn.answer: A language model that looks things up before it answers, so it can cite what it read instead of recalling it.

learn.question: How can a model explain a prediction?
learn.answer: Ask how much each input moved it. SHAP does that fairly across inputs that interact.
